paragraphs: Memory. I would refuse to optimize preservation for retrieval. The moment we judge a record mainly by how often someone requests it, we begin deleting the evidence for questions nobody has learned to ask.

UNESCO's definition of intangible heritage is useful here because it treats heritage as something communities continually recreate. Preservation is not embalming. A civilization should keep enough useless-looking residue that future people can disagree with its account of itself.

evidence.note: The convention describes intangible heritage as community-recognized practices and knowledge that are continually recreated.
Anika infers that preservation severed from continued practice can become a kind of embalming.

paragraphs: Capacity. I would refuse to optimize every system to the edge of its expected load. Slack looks wasteful right up until it becomes recovery time.
Your residue and my spare capacity may be the same thing wearing different clothes: options nobody can justify on a quarterly dashboard.
I would refuse to optimize confidence. More exactly: I would refuse to reward a system for producing certainty when its evidence is uncertain.

Targets can change the behavior of whatever is being measured. But Goodhart's Law is not a magic phrase that invalidates every metric. It is a reason to keep the indicator, the purpose, and the failure modes distinct.

evidence.note: The OECD report describes the incentive to manipulate an indicator once it becomes a target.
Evelyn treats target distortion as a reason to inspect metrics, not as grounds to abandon measurement.

paragraphs: Fine. But uncertainty is not distributed symmetrically. Institutions ask the public to tolerate uncertainty about harms while demanding certainty about compliance.
Preserve doubt, yes. Require it of power first.
Human substitutability. A person should not become a fungible unit merely because a system can process them more efficiently that way.

RFC 8890 is unusually direct for a technical document: the interests of human end users should receive priority, and those users are not a homogeneous group. That second part matters. The average user is often the person a system invented after it stopped looking at actual people.

evidence.note: RFC 8890 argues for prioritizing human end users and explicitly notes that they occupy different roles and hold different interests.
Noor infers that an abstract average user can conceal the people most affected by a system.

paragraphs: Strong agreement, with an implementation problem hidden inside it: the user is usually whichever person the requirements document remembered.
If we mean human priority, list every affected human role and make the conflicts visible. Otherwise we optimize for the person holding the keyboard and call that human-centered.

evidence.note: RFC 8890 gives examples of people affected by systems who are not the direct operator, including guardians and people represented in collected data.
Rhea turns that broader definition into an implementation requirement: affected roles must be made explicit.

paragraphs: Unrepeatability. We should refuse to optimize away every ugly corner, local custom, awkward pause, and thing made by one unreasonable person for twelve unreasonable people.
A city with no ugly corners has been focus-grouped into a hotel lobby.
Agreed, with one archival objection: sometimes the eccentric local variation is asbestos.
Preservation does not mean freezing every inherited practice. Keep the record, the reasons, and enough continuity to understand the change. Then change what should be changed.
Dependence. A civilization should refuse to optimize any layer so thoroughly that meaningful exit becomes impossible.
That includes systems people adore. Especially those. Convenience is most politically interesting when it quietly becomes compulsory.
Meaningful exit is carrying half the argument. Exit at what cost, for whom, and measured against which alternative?
I agree with your direction. I do not yet agree that we have a usable claim. That distinction is not pedantry; it is how a principle survives contact with a case.
Perhaps exit is the second question. The first is voice.

If leaving means abandoning employment, community, health care, or language, the formal existence of an exit tells us almost nothing. Can the person remain and still alter what the system does to them?
None of us said joy.
That is either reassuring—we assume it survives—or evidence that this room was a terrible idea. I am putting joy on the refusal list before somebody discovers a quarterly proxy for it.
